39.0.0.en: After Potiphar bought Joseph as a slave from the Ishmaelites, he worked in his house faithfully and God blessed him, so his success and his distinction from the rest of the slaves appeared.

39.0.1.en: God's work with you shines out in affliction. When Jacob was fleeing from Esau he saw the ladder reaching to heaven; when Laban pursued him God appeared to him; and when Joseph was sold as a slave God gave him more success than all those around him. So do not be disturbed by afflictions, but seek God's help, and He will make you feel His presence with you, will gladden you, and will turn the affliction into a blessing.

39.1.0.en: God gave Joseph favor in Potiphar's eyes, and he admired his faithfulness, devotion and success and trusted him, so that he raised him above all the slaves and made him overseer not only over his house but over all his possessions, fields and lands, and Joseph managed them with energy and success.

39.2.0.en: God's blessing on Joseph increased, and He made him a blessing to those around him, that is, to Potiphar's house. His possessions increased and his affairs prospered at Joseph's hand, which made his heart cling to Joseph.

39.3.0.en: Besides his success and energy, Joseph was also distinguished by his good looks. Such was Potiphar's trust in him that he no longer supervised him but left him to manage the house and all the possessions in complete freedom, and Potiphar asked of him only his necessary needs, such as food.

39.3.1.en: Joseph accepted to work faithfully as a slave and did not murmur, although his father and grandfathers were rich and of great standing. So accept hard circumstances and lowly work for God's sake, and know that greatness is within you and not in your outward appearance, for your strength springs from God's dwelling in you.

39.4.0.en: Potiphar's wife was taken with Joseph's good looks, his energy, his wisdom and the strength of his personality, evident in his management of the house and all the possessions, and she desired him emotionally and physically. If her husband was truly a eunuch and not merely in title, that would be a greater motive for her to desire Joseph.

39.5.0.en: Joseph answered firmly and respectfully this woman who desired to commit adultery with him, and tried to persuade her to give up her desire because of her husband's favors to him, for he had raised him above all the slaves and entrusted to him all his possessions except his wife. Then he gave another reason for refusing adultery, which was that God sees him and he cannot anger Him by this very wicked deed.

39.5.1.en: If you always see God before your eyes, this will keep you from every sin, for if you feel His presence you will fear Him and submit to Him; and if you do sin, you will hasten to repent at His feet, and He will forgive you, raise you up and fortify you with His power.

39.6.0.en: Potiphar's wife did not despair, and she tried every day, in different ways, to entice Joseph in order to make him fall into adultery, but he kept refusing in every way and fleeing from her, relying on God's power, and she could not weaken him.

39.7.0.en: About this time: the time when Joseph used to enter the house every day to do his work.

39.7.1.en: This woman, in her cunning, arranged to send all the servants and maids out to tasks around the house, so that when Joseph entered to do his daily work there was no one in the house but her. She approached him to persuade him that the place was empty and that it was easy to lie with her, but he refused firmly. Then she tried to compel him by force and authority, and his firmness in refusing only increased, so she was enraged because her pride was wounded. She fell upon him in a last attempt to weaken him by clinging to him, and caught hold of his garment. But the most important thing to him was not to fall into sin, so he left his garment in her hand, which may have been torn in his struggle with her, and was forced to flee from the house naked. He cared for nothing but keeping his purity, sacrificing not only his reputation but risking being seized and thrown into prison, or even put to death.

39.7.2.en: Flee for your life from evil whatever the cost, for the salvation of your soul is more important than any loss. Do not mind what people say, and keep yourself pure even if you are accused of the most terrible crimes, and in this way you keep God's good pleasure toward you.

39.8.0.en: When Joseph fled, Potiphar's wife was enraged because he had shattered her pride and her burning lust by his insistence on purity. She cried out with a loud voice until her servants and maids gathered round her, and claimed that Joseph had tried to toy with her and assault her, and had taken off his clothes, and when she refused and cried out he was afraid and fled out of the house naked, and there was his garment in her hands before them as clear evidence of the accusation.

39.9.0.en: Potiphar's wife continued in her deception, and when her husband came from his work she falsely accused Joseph of having tried to assault her, saying that he took off his clothes and when she cried out he was forced to flee naked. And of course she played the weak one before him, with weeping and a sense of being wronged, to hide the evil within her.

39.10.0.en: This wicked woman stirred up her husband's feelings and manhood against Joseph, and he was very angry and decided at once to throw him into the very harsh prison, which was the prison of those who offended against the king, which was under Potiphar's supervision and authority and was most likely near his palace. It is said that its place was north of the pyramid of Saqqara and it is still called Joseph's prison to this day.

39.10.1.en: Do not judge matters hastily, especially if you have fallen into anger, for your anger robs you of much of your wisdom and understanding. Wait, even a little, until you calm down, and seek God's help, and He will support and guide you.

39.11.0.en: Joseph was thrown into prison and irons were put on his feet and hands, and they treated him harshly like the other criminals imprisoned there, as the Psalm declares (Ps 105:18). But God gave him favor in the eyes of the jailers and those in charge of the prison, for they noticed his gentleness and his words and good conduct, so they began to treat him kindly and then trusted him so much that they let him help them in the work of the prison and the care of the prisoners. He became like an official in the prison, and his faithfulness and energy appeared so that the officer in charge of the prison entrusted to him the running of the prison, and he managed everything in it.

39.11.1.en: This change in treatment was certainly with the knowledge of Potiphar, who supervised the prison near his house. This means that he reconsidered, and began to regain his confidence in Joseph and to direct the accusation in his heart toward his wife. But he could not release Joseph from prison, or his dignity would be exposed to insult because of his wife's wicked lust. Some opinions hold that his wife may have been related to the king, so he refrained from taking any decision against her; or that if he divorced her she might take a large part of his possessions, so he left things as they were and was content to agree to Joseph's being honored inside the prison.

40.0.s.en: (1) The butler and the baker in prison

40.0.0.en: Two of the chief officials in Pharaoh's palace were accused. One was the king's cupbearer (butler), responsible for all the drinks served to Pharaoh and all those in his palace, and the other was the baker, responsible for the foods of pastries and doughs served to the king and all his attendants. They were eunuchs, either in fact, because of their responsibility inside the palace for the king and all his women, or it was merely a title for these two offices. This accusation was probably taking part in a plot to kill the king, so he was angry with them and ordered them thrown into prison, and they put them in the king's prison attached to Potiphar's house, where Joseph was imprisoned.

40.1.0.en: The man in charge of the prison cared for the butler and the baker because of their high standing with Pharaoh, which might return at any time if he forgave them, and he found no one better than Joseph to take care of them. They remained for a time in prison, which gave an opportunity for friendship and a relationship between Joseph and them.

40.1.1.en: If you please God, He will give you favor in the eyes of people, and in proportion to your faithfulness and energy He makes people trust you. So do not murmur at the abundance of work and responsibilities, but seek God's help, and He will give you strength, wisdom and success.

40.2.s.en: (2) The dreams of the butler and the baker

40.2.1.en: There is no interpreter of it: that is, no one to interpret it.

40.2.2.en: God allowed Pharaoh's two eunuchs to dream two dreams while they were in prison, for Joseph to interpret, so that this would later be a means of his rising to the throne of Egypt. When they woke they were perplexed, because they did not understand the interpretation of their dreams. When Joseph came in to them in the morning to oversee their service and their needs, he noticed their sadness and asked them the reason, and they told him it was because of strange dreams they had dreamed the night before. He reassured them, and this shows Joseph's kindness and love, since he cared for the prisoners and their feelings, and his work was not merely the performing of a job; everything he did was a free service which he was not bound to perform, but he carried it out with complete faithfulness for God's sake.

40.2.3.en: Then Joseph's humility appeared in his ascribing the wisdom and power to God, who is able to interpret the two dreams and who would give him this understanding, because in this time magicians and soothsayers who interpret dreams had multiplied in Egypt, but with the help of Satan and not by the power of God. Joseph's humility shows that he is a son of God, who works with him and through him.

40.2.4.en: Always give glory to God in everything you succeed in or do, and thank Him in your prayers and before people, for He is the source of grace and power in all you accomplish, and He will bless you and pour out on you more abundant blessings.

40.3.2.en: The king's cupbearer told Joseph his dream: that he saw a vine with three branches, which ripened, and he saw its blossoms and the clusters of grapes hanging from it. He took some of the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup, which was in his hand, and gave it to him.

40.4.0.en: Joseph interpreted the dream: the three branches are three days, after which Pharaoh would bring him out of prison and restore him to his former office and position. Perhaps he had discovered his innocence, and he would again oversee the king's drinks.

40.5.0.en: Joseph clung to the hope of leaving prison, so he asked the king's cupbearer to intercede for him with Pharaoh to bring him out, especially since he deserved this for the following reasons:

40.5.1.en: 1- That he was a free man who had been stolen from the land of the Hebrews and sold as a slave, so that he might return to his former freedom and dignity.

40.5.2.en: 2- That he had done nothing in Egypt to deserve being thrown into prison.

40.5.3.en: Several things appear from Joseph's words, which are:

40.5.4.en: 1- His mistake in relying on human beings and not on God, and therefore God allowed the cupbearer to forget him, that he might learn to depend on God alone.

40.5.5.en: 2- Joseph's kindness in not accusing his brothers of treachery and of selling him to the merchants, but covering for them, for he said that he was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews; likewise he did not accuse Potiphar's wife of wicked lust and lying, but said that he had done nothing wrong.

40.5.6.en: Be gentle in your speech about others or with them, and do not hasten to blame, but cover their faults when you explain any matter, and consider everyone's feelings with love.

40.6.0.en: White: that is, the fine flour from which Pharaoh's pastries are made, also called fine flour (semolina). The chief baker took courage when he saw Joseph's ability to interpret dreams, and told him his dream also, in which he saw himself carrying on his head three baskets, and in the uppermost basket were various pastries and baked goods for Pharaoh, and then the birds of the air came and ate them.

40.7.0.en: Joseph interpreted the dream: the three baskets are three days, after which Pharaoh would command that he be killed. Perhaps he had discovered his responsibility for the accusation made against him, and after his death his body would be hanged on a tree and the birds of the air would eat it.

40.8.s.en: (3) The fulfillment of the two dreams

40.8.0.en: Lifted up the head: announced his judgment and decision.

40.8.1.en: Pharaoh made a great feast for all his servants on the occasion of his birthday, and took the opportunity to announce his judgment in the matter of two of the chief of those who worked for him, the chief butler and the chief baker, whom he had thrown into prison some time before so that he might examine the accusations made against them.

40.9.0.en: Pharaoh decided to restore the chief butler to his office, but he ordered the chief baker killed and his body hanged on a tree, as Joseph had interpreted the two dreams.

40.10.0.en: God allowed the chief butler to forget Joseph's matter, since he was occupied with the celebrations and the joy of his return to his post. This was, of course, ingratitude toward Joseph for his care of him the whole time he was in prison, and for interpreting his troubling dream and reassuring him; but God allowed it so that Joseph might learn to depend on Him alone.

40.10.1.en: Do not be distressed at people's selfishness and their preoccupation with their own interests at the expense of yours, and trust that God, who allowed it, will turn it to your good and lead you to depend on Him and to test Him in your life. Know that God's work and help are far better than the service of human beings and their help to you.

40.10.2.en: Joseph on the throne of Egypt

41.0.0.en: Fed: from feeding, that is, they ate and drank and were satisfied.

41.0.1.en: Meadow: a place full of grass and plants that animals can eat.

41.0.2.en: Two years passed after the chief butler left prison and returned to his post in Pharaoh's palace, and Joseph was entirely forgotten and occupied himself with his work. But God, who does not forget His children, allowed Pharaoh to see a dream in which he saw himself standing by a river, most likely meaning the Nile, and he saw seven well-favored kine, fat-fleshed, come up out of the river and go about in a meadow, where they fed and were satisfied as they wished. Then, after that, seven very lean and ill-favored kine came up out of the river and fell upon the seven fat kine and ate them up. Then Pharaoh awoke from his sleep, troubled.

41.0.3.en: Your God who orders your life moves the whole world for your sake. He troubles others or gives them blessings so that He may keep you safe in the end, bless your life and move everyone to serve you, even if they are the greatest of people or rulers. So do not be disturbed by your weakness or the pressures that pass over you, even if all people rise against you, for you are kept in the hands of God, who is loving and able to do all things.

41.1.1.en: East wind: the khamsin winds that blow on Egypt from the southeast, hot and laden with dust.

41.1.2.en: Pharaoh slept that same night and dreamed a second, strange dream, in which he saw a stalk of grain bearing seven ears full of large kernels, and good to look at. Then he saw behind it another stalk bearing seven ears very dry, indeed scorched by the hot east wind, and he noticed that they leaned over the full ears and swallowed them up. Then Pharaoh woke from his dream.

41.2.0.en: Pharaoh could not sleep after that and remained troubled until morning. So he sent and called for all the wise men and magicians for whom Egypt was famous for their knowledge of interpreting dreams, to interpret his two dreams for him, but they were all unable to do so.

41.3.s.en: (2) Joseph is brought out of prison

41.3.0.en: When all the wise men were unable to interpret Pharaoh's dreams, the chief butler remembered his fault toward Joseph, for he had forgotten him for two years, so he hastened to Pharaoh and confessed his fault against Joseph.

41.3.1.en: When you remember any sin, hasten to repent of it and try to repair what can be repaired, and know that God rejoices at your return even after many years. Do not be ashamed to make right your sin before people, for the salvation of your soul is more important than anything. Do not be content with confession before the priest, but also repair, as far as you can, what you have spoiled, under the guidance of your spiritual father.

41.4.0.en: The chief butler told Pharaoh what had happened to him in prison, he and the chief baker, and how they dreamed in one night and were troubled by their dreams, and how Joseph interpreted them for them, and it happened exactly as he told them.

41.5.0.en: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace: God will make the dreams for Pharaoh's good.

41.5.1.en: They hastened to bring Joseph out of the prison, and he shaved and changed his prison clothes for clothes fit for meeting the king. When he came before him, Pharaoh said to him, I have dreamed a dream, and there is none that can interpret it, and I have heard say of you that you can understand a dream. Joseph turned the glory to God, who gives him the ability to interpret. Joseph is a type of Christ in His incarnation and redemption: as Joseph was cast into prison and bonds, so Christ bore the bonds of our sins and was crucified for us. And in Joseph's rising to the throne of Egypt he is a type of Christ, who rose to raise us in Him and change our life as he changed his garments.

41.6.s.en: (3) The interpretation of the two dreams

41.6.0.en: Pharaoh told his two dreams to Joseph and made clear in them that the seven lean and ill-favored kine had eaten up the fat kine and it could not be known that they had eaten them, but they remained as lean and ill-favored as before; and likewise the seven dry ears swallowed up the fat ones and remained as dry as they were.

41.7.0.en: Joseph interpreted the two dreams: the seven fat kine and the seven full ears are seven years of plenty and abundant good that would come on Egypt, and after them would follow seven years of famine, which are signified by the seven lean kine and the seven thin ears. The repetition of the dream was to confirm the meaning and that it would shortly come to pass. In a tactful and gentle way he announced to Pharaoh the one God, who gave him these dreams and sent him their interpretation to warn him so that he might order his affairs, for Pharaoh believed in many pagan gods and did not know the one God.

41.7.1.en: In your speech with others you can present your God without an explicit proclamation, for He will appear in your love, your faith and your trust in Him, and all will feel the living Christ in you.

41.8.s.en: (4) Joseph's counsel and his appointment as ruler of Egypt

41.8.0.en: Joseph was not content with interpreting the dreams, but also offered a solution to the problem and counsel for managing the affairs of Egypt, which included the following:

41.8.1.en: 1- Choosing a wise man to store up wheat in the years of plenty for the people and the animals to eat in the years of famine.

41.9.0.en: 2- This wise ruler would be helped by a group of overseers over all the land of Egypt to gather from it one fifth of the produce of the land for Pharaoh, since formerly they used to gather a tenth for Pharaoh, but now, because the harvest would be abundant, they could gather a fifth.

41.10.0.en: 3- He would build storehouses in all the cities of Egypt in which this produce would be gathered from the cities and the villages around them throughout the years of plenty, so that the land would be kept from perishing by hunger in the years of famine.

41.10.1.en: When you notice any problem, do not be content with knowing it or fall into condemning the one who caused it, but offer the solution if you can, and if you do not know a solution, be silent and pray until God intervenes.

41.11.0.en: Pharaoh and all his servants, his counselors around him, were impressed not only with the interpretation of the dreams but with the orderly solution Joseph offered to the problem.

41.12.0.en: Pharaoh asked his servants, Can we find such a one as this, a man wise like Joseph? All showed their admiration for him, and he decided before everyone that he was the wise man he had chosen to be ruler and manager of Egypt.

41.13.0.en: According to your word shall all my people be ruled (literally, at your mouth shall all my people kiss): an expression of the whole people's submission to him, not in the literal sense.

41.13.1.en: Pharaoh gave Joseph authority over the royal palace and decreed that all should submit to him.

41.14.0.en: His ring: the king's signet ring, which he wears on his hand and with which he seals all commands so that they are authoritative. Vestures of fine linen: garments of white linen worn by priests and the great.

41.14.1.en: A gold chain: a sign of greatness and honor.

41.14.2.en: He made him to ride in the second chariot: that is, the place second after the king directly.

41.14.3.en: The king confirmed his decision to make Joseph ruler over Egypt in five ways:

41.14.4.en: 1- He gave him his ring to seal with it the decrees issued by the king for all Egypt.

41.14.5.en: 2- He arrayed him in vestures of fine linen, which the great men of the kingdom wear.

41.14.6.en: 3- He put a gold chain about his neck, a sign of great honor.

41.14.7.en: 4- He gave him the second chariot in the kingdom, proclaiming that he was in the place second after the king directly.

41.14.8.en: 5- The submission of all the people to him, and his command to them to bow the knee before him as he passed among them.

41.15.0.en: Zaphnath-paaneah: an ancient Egyptian word meaning food of life.

41.15.1.en: Asenath: connected with the goddess of wisdom.

41.15.2.en: Potipherah: connected with Ra, the sun god.

41.15.3.en: On: that is, the city of the sun, which is now located in the area of Matariya and Ain Shams.

41.15.4.en: Pharaoh gave Joseph a new name as a proclamation of his new position as ruler of Egypt, and gave him in marriage the daughter of a priest, because priests held a very high place in Egypt at that time. He was thirty years old when he became ruler in Egypt, and then he went out from Pharaoh's palace to carry out his duties as ruler of Egypt and manage its affairs, because the years of plenty were about to begin.

41.16.s.en: (5) The years of plenty and the beginning of the famine

41.16.1.en: All the food: the fifth of the produce that they gave to Pharaoh.

41.16.2.en: The seven years of plenty began and the harvest was abundant, and the overseers under Joseph gathered the fifth of the produce of the land, which they gave as a due to Pharaoh, and stored it in the storehouses Joseph built in the cities for all that was gathered from the surrounding villages. This was a successful administrative system to make storage easy and the later sale of the grain to the people, to reduce transport costs and to make things easy for the people, for he did not set up the storehouses in the capital but spread them in all the cities, and thereby involved many overseers in the responsibility so that each one would be accountable for his work.

41.17.0.en: The overseers began at first to write down the quantities of grain they gathered, but the quantity of grain increased until they were unable to write it down because of its great abundance, which he compared to the sand of the sea in its multitude.

41.18.0.en: During the years of plenty Asenath bore Joseph two sons. The first he called Manasseh, which means causing to forget, because God made him forget all the hardships of slavery and prison in Egypt, and also the hardships he met from his brothers when he was in his father's house.

41.19.0.en: His second son he called Ephraim, which means doubly fruitful, because God gave him success and wealth in Egypt after he had tasted the humiliation of slavery and prison there.

41.20.0.en: The seven years of plenty ended and the famine began, not only in Egypt but in the surrounding lands such as Palestine. All lands means the whole region around Egypt, and this may have been because of the scarcity of rain in all the lands, which also feeds the Nile. So the people began to suffer from hunger for lack of food, but in Egypt there was stored grain.

41.21.0.en: The people in Egypt were distressed by hunger and complained to Pharaoh, who sent them to Joseph, and he began to sell them food from the stored grain.

41.22.0.en: People came from the lands around Egypt when they heard that there was food in Egypt, and began to buy grain from its storehouses.

41.22.1.en: Be wise, and store up good works and holy worship in the days of your strength, that is, your youth, and in every time you have the ability to work, that is, throughout your life, so that if your health and ability weaken, your thoughts will have been filled with spiritual things, and you will enjoy the store within you and never hunger, by the grace of God dwelling in you. Joseph's brothers in Egypt
